source_summary.design: Three-wave longitudinal panel survey in the Netherlands (Kieskompas research panels; not preregistered), analysed with cross-lagged panel models (CLPM) and random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM). Wave 1 April 2020 (first lockdown), Wave 2 June 2020 (between lockdowns), Wave 3 December 2020 (second lockdown). The authors state that the longitudinal design cannot prove causality.
source_summary.sample: N = 4913 Dutch respondents who took part in all three waves (Wave 1 N = 9033, Wave 2 N = 6775, Wave 3 N = 5745); 3516 men and 1397 women; mean age 59.68 (SD 14.45); N = 4118 in the models because of missing values. Men were overrepresented and belief in conspiracy theories was low.
source_summary.measures: Belief in nine Covid-19 conspiracy theories common in the Netherlands in 2020 (credibility ratings, 1-5; alpha .84-.86); self-reported physical distancing (4 items, 0-10); support for lockdown policy (5 items, 0-10); perceived danger of the coronavirus (3 items, 1-5).
source_summary.main_results: CLPM: stronger conspiracy beliefs predicted decreases in physical distancing and in perceived danger at the next wave (all cross-lagged paths significant). These paths were larger than the also-significant reverse paths (Wald tests). Conspiracy beliefs predicted reduced lockdown support only from Wave 2 to Wave 3. RI-CLPM (within-person): conspiracy beliefs predicted decreased distancing only from Wave 1 to 2, and decreased perceived danger only from Wave 2 to 3. Perceived danger at Wave 1 predicted increased conspiracy beliefs, and the within-person lockdown-support paths were paradoxically positive. Conclusion: stronger support for the hypothesis that conspiracy beliefs predict health responses than for the reverse, with within-person effects that depend on the outcome and the phase of the pandemic.

occurrences.explanation: The quoted words are verbatim from the source's last Discussion sentence ('Apparently, conspiracy theories predict deteriorated health responses to Covid-19 throughout the course of the pandemic'). The framing is accurate: a three-wave longitudinal panel in the Netherlands (April, June and December 2020; N = 4913, 'a large Dutch panel ... at three time points', p. 5710). The wording is predictive, not causal, as in the source, and the direction (conspiracy beliefs -> worse health responses) is right. The only error is the page locator. The sentence is on printed p. 5715 (PDF p. 7), not p. 5713. Page 5713 reports the RI-CLPM physical-distancing results and the lockdown-support results, and the quoted sentence is not there. A nuance that needs no change: the sentence is the authors' hedged ('Apparently') summary for the first pandemic year only, and their detailed results are qualified. Between-person effects ran in both directions for distancing and perceived danger, though larger from conspiracy beliefs to health responses. The lockdown-support effect appeared only from June to December 2020. Within-person effects depended on the outcome and phase, as the source itself says on the same page.

evidence.quote: Apparently, conspiracy theories predict deteriorated health responses to Covid-19 throughout the course of the pandemic.

Conspiracy beliefs predicted more detrimental health beliefs and behaviors over time, although within-person changes differed across outcome variables and depended on the specific phase of the pandemic.
